primary_topics: Chapter 1 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' -- the substantive part of CJP's paper 'Speeding up Quality Justice,' written as chairman of the Supreme Court Committee on Public Information, tracing the causes of judicial delay and the solutions meant to deliver not merely swift but fair and impartial justice.

The statistical picture: the Supreme Court has been outdisposing its own filings and should reach 'zero backlog' by its centenary on June 11, 2001, while the Court of Appeals, Sandiganbayan and especially the trial courts accumulate cases year after year.

A two-part diagnosis of delay -- systemic causes arising from the very system of governance (due process mechanics, an open-ended appellate system, BP 22 collection cases, automatic death appeals, review of constitutional bodies, administrative supervision) and man-made causes traceable to judges, lawyers, litigants and court personnel.

The three families of solutions -- better selection, education and compensation of judges; upgraded judicial tools, facilities and management; and systemic reforms such as ADR, discovery, small claims courts and filtered appeals -- all resting on the common denominator of transparency and accountability.
sub_topics: He opens with a catalogue of the grounds on which justices and judges have been disciplined, from arrogance and ignorance to corruption and 'pesky' illegal TROs, and argues that sanctions alone cannot elevate standards -- prevention and positive solutions matter more.
Delay is the easiest problem to demonstrate, provable by statistics, said to breed corruption and partiality, and caused not only by malevolent intent but by incompetence and negligence.

He explains that the chapter reproduces the substantive part of his paper 'Speeding up Quality Justice,' printed, broadcast and debated two months earlier, and that he will neither deny nor excuse the fact of delay.
Supreme Court statistics for 1995-1999 show 4,337 cases filed on average against 4,506 disposed of, with 1999 alone ending 792 cases ahead of filings.

Backlog means cases pending beyond the twenty-four months Article VIII, Section 15 of the Constitution allows the Court; it stood at about 6,000 after EDSA, 2,000 in Battles in the Supreme Court, and about 1,000 at writing -- so 'zero backlog' would fittingly mark the Court's 100th anniversary.

The lower courts move the other way: the Court of Appeals grew by 3,088 cases over five years, the Sandiganbayan by a marginal 35, the second-level courts by 33,975, and the first-level courts by 'a humongous total of 324,174.'

Court Administrator Alfredo L. Benipayo's figures go back to 1991 and show the disposition rate falling from 39.70 per cent to 25.50 per cent, leaving the lower courts a 'gargantuan caseload totalling 801,625' entering 2000.
He endorses CJ Davide's goal under the 'Davide Watch' of 'fair, impartial and swift justice,' insisting that speed without evenhandedness 'would be railroading tyranny to our hapless people.'

Systemic cause one: the adversarial system itself requires due process -- Frankfurter's 'embodiment of the sporting idea of fair play,' Themistocles' 'Strike if you must, but hear me first,' Webster's hearing before condemning -- and its mechanics, from summonses to personally written decisions, all take time.

Systemic causes two to six: an open-ended appellate system that draws trivial cases to the Highest Court, BP 22 collection cases flooding first-level courts, roughly three thousand automatic appeals of death, reclusion perpetua and life sentences, review of the Comelec, COA and Ombudsman, and administrative supervision over all courts and lawyers.

Man-made delays come from judges unfamiliar with procedure, lazy or corrupt judges, about 33 percent of trial court salas left vacant because able lawyers shun the bench, lawyers who 'use, misuse and abuse the Rules of Court,' and clerks, sheriffs, interpreters and process servers.

Solutions beginning with the judges: reform of law schools and curricula, a private foundation for faculty chairs and scholarships, a Committee on Legal Education, a Study Group on Bar Reforms, and a JBC screening process made more transparent by three innovations proposed by Sen. Aquilino Q. Pimentel Jr.

Continuing education through the Philippine Judicial Academy under retired Justice Ameurfina A. Melencio-Herrera, which needs some P500 million for its Tagaytay plant, and the RA 8557 pre-judicature course required of all applicants from January 1, 2001.

Compensation and fiscal independence: exemption from the Salary Standardization Law, and a lump-sum appropriation of a fixed percentage -- say two percent -- of a national budget of which the judiciary now receives less than one percent (P6.28 billion of over P665 billion).

The disciplinary process needs review: more than forty judges dismissed in two years and twice that number suspended or fined, yet a long and strict process treats frivolous and meritorious complaints alike while blocking promotion and retirement benefits.

Judicial tools and facilities: more Halls of Justice (Manila has yet to build one), computerization of administrative services and legal research, the Internet homepage www.supremecourt.gov.ph, and 1,500 computers for distribution to trial courts within 2000.

Judicial management: more than 25,000 personnel are supervised by a collegial Court whose business is decision-making, so day-to-day management falls to the Office of the Court Administrator -- yet 'eminent jurists do not necessarily make excellent administrators,' and judicial administration should become a career in itself.

Ten systemic solutions: ADR, discovery and active pretrial settlement, small claims courts below P50,000, mandatory continuous trial, decriminalization of bouncing checks, filtering capital appeals through the Court of Appeals, proactive management of procedures, updating the Rules of Court for paperless pleadings, Bantay Katarungan and the Foundation for Judicial Excellence, and the Judicial Reforms Committee of Philja.

The common denominator: transparency and accountability -- some judicial work must stay confidential, but opening 'heretofore sacrosanct areas to public scrutiny' makes judges' actions not only pure but seen to be pure, and has attracted UNDP, World Bank, AusAID, USAID, JICA, ADB, the Asia Foundation and CIDA.

stances.claim: Sanctions against erring judges are necessary but not enough to elevate the standards of judicial dispensation; it is more important to prevent the problems and to implement positive solutions for swift, objective and evenhanded justice.
stances.rhetorical_move: opening catalogue of offenses used to set up a prevention-over-punishment thesis

stances.claim: Delay in the delivery of justice is a given and will not be denied or excused; the honest course is to trace its causes and report what the Court is doing about them.
stances.rhetorical_move: candor-as-credibility opening, refusing excuses before offering an explanation

stances.claim: The goal cannot be merely swift justice but fair and impartial justice, since speed without evenhandedness 'would be railroading tyranny to our hapless people.'
stances.rhetorical_move: corrective qualification of the reform slogan, sharpened by a vivid consequence

stances.claim: The Supreme Court is winning against its own backlog while the lower courts fall further behind, so the crisis of delay is concentrated below and will worsen unless the declining disposition rate is reversed.
stances.rhetorical_move: comparative statistics across five years and four court levels

stances.claim: Judicial compensation must be rationalized through exemption from the Salary Standardization Law and real fiscal independence by way of a lump-sum appropriation fixed as a percentage of the national budget.
stances.rhetorical_move: budget arithmetic -- less than one percent of P665 billion -- driving a structural proposal

stances.claim: Judicial administration should become a career in itself, because eminent jurists do not necessarily make excellent administrators and management is a distinct discipline with its own science and art.
stances.rhetorical_move: role-differentiation argument contrasting the loner jurist with the team-building manager

stances.claim: Transparency and accountability are the common denominator underlying every solution to delay, because public understanding of the judiciary makes judges' actions not only pure but seen to be pure.
stances.rhetorical_move: synthesizing close that names a single governing policy behind the whole program

notable_anecdotes: He explains that this first chapter reproduces the substantive part of his own paper 'Speeding up Quality Justice,' which had been printed by many dailies, discussed on radio and television, and debated in judicial and bar circles.
He dates his own seat on the Court -- assumed October 10, 1995 -- to explain why his statistics begin with 1995.
He tracks his own running estimate of the backlog across his books: about 6,000 after EDSA, about 2,000 in Battles in the Supreme Court, and about 1,000 now.
He breaks the statistical narration with an aside at the second-level courts' 33,975-case increase: 'Now, that's a lot of cases!'
He notes with surprise that the City of Manila has yet to build a Hall of Justice.
He recalls reporting the Court's information-technology tools in his March 10, 2000 address to the Manila Overseas Press Club, and refers the reader there rather than repeating them.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' reproduces the substantive part of Panganiban's paper 'Speeding up Quality Justice,' written as chairman of the Supreme Court Committee on Public Information. He opens with the grounds on which judges have been disciplined -- arrogance, ignorance, incompetence, dishonesty, delay, corruption, partiality and 'pesky' illegal TROs -- and argues that sanctions alone cannot raise standards. Refusing to deny or excuse delay, he sets out the statistics: from 1995 to 1999 the Supreme Court disposed of more cases than were filed, reducing a post-EDSA backlog of about 6,000 to roughly 1,000, so that 'zero backlog' could fittingly mark its centenary on June 11, 2001. The lower courts run the other way, the first-level courts alone growing by 'a humongous total of 324,174,' with Court Administrator Benipayo reporting a disposition rate falling to 25.50 percent and a caseload of 801,625. Endorsing Chief Justice Davide's aim of fair, impartial and swift justice, he insists speed without evenhandedness 'would be railroading tyranny to our hapless people.' He classifies causes as systemic -- the adversarial system's due-process mechanics, an open-ended appellate system, BP 22 collection cases, thousands of automatic capital appeals, review of constitutional bodies, and supervision of all courts and lawyers -- and man-made, from unfamiliar or corrupt judges and 33 percent vacant salas to lawyers who abuse the Rules and dilatory court personnel. His solutions run in three lines: reforming law schools, bar examinations, JBC screening, Philja education and the RA 8557 pre-judicature course, plus rationalized compensation through exemption from the Salary Standardization Law and real fiscal independence; upgrading Halls of Justice, computers and the Court's website, and professionalizing judicial administration; and systemic measures from ADR and discovery to small claims courts, continuous trial, decriminalized bouncing checks and filtered capital appeals. The common denominator, he concludes, is transparency and accountability.
